1000488.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Jón (“male given name”), a contraction of earlier Jóann, from Latin Iōhannēs, from Ancient Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs), from Biblical Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (Yōḥānān, “Yahweh is gracious”).
Doublet of Jan, Johan, Johannes, Jens, and Hans.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Jon, Danish Jon, Swedish Jon, Icelandic Jón and Faroese Jón (“male given name”).

1001256.etyen:
Borrowed from English Annie (“female given name”), adapted in spelling. English Annie is a pet form of Ann and Anne. The name ultimately derives from Late Latin Anna (“female given name”), from Koine Greek Ἄννα (Ánna, “Anna”), from Biblical Hebrew חַנָּה (“grace, favour”), from Biblical Hebrew חָנַן (“to be gracious, show favour”).
The spelling was already in use in Norway in the 19th century.
Compare Danish Anni and Swedish Anni (“female given name”).

The one who speaks a little more / and who seems quite content / is a female Lutheran.

1005096.etyen:
From lutheraner (“Lutheran”) + -inne (“feminine noun-forming suffix”), ultimately named after the German theologian Martin Luther.
The base lutheraner derives through German Luther, Old High German Liutheri, Proto-West Germanic *liudi and *hari, Proto-Germanic *liudiz and *harjaz, and ultimately Proto-Indo-European *h₁léwdʰis and *kóryos. Its suffix -aner derives through Latin -ānus, Proto-Italic *-ānos and Proto-Indo-European *-nós.
The suffix -inne continues Old Norse -inna, borrowed from Middle Low German -inne and -in, ultimately from Old Saxon -ina and -unnia, Proto-West Germanic *-ini an
